title: Aledade: overview and enablement model
questions: What is Aledade?
Does Aledade own primary care clinics?
Who does Aledade work with?
What kind of company is Aledade?
summary: Aledade is a physician-led value-based care enablement company founded in 2014 and headquartered in Bethesda, Maryland. It does not own or employ practices. Instead it forms and operates accountable care organizations (ACOs) that independent primary care practices, federally qualified health centers and community health centers join while keeping their ownership. Aledade supplies data and analytics software, care-management workflows, practice-level support staff and payer contracting, and the ACO enters value-based contracts with Medicare (chiefly the Medicare Shared Savings Program), Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid and commercial payers. The company describes itself as a public benefit corporation. Its co-founders are Farzad Mostashari, a former National Coordinator for Health IT who serves as CEO, and Mat Kendall, who serves as President. Aledade is privately held and venture-backed. In the market it is the archetype of the independent-practice enablement model, in contrast to owned-clinic operators such as Oak Street Health or ChenMed and to full-risk Medicare Advantage partnership models such as agilon health.

title: How Aledade makes money
questions: How does Aledade make money?
Do practices pay Aledade a fee?
How are shared savings split between Aledade and practices?
Who bears downside risk in Aledade ACOs?
summary: Aledade's revenue comes mainly from its share of the savings its ACOs earn under value-based contracts. In the Medicare Shared Savings Program, CMS pays an ACO a portion of the spending it holds below a benchmark if quality standards are met; Aledade's ACOs then distribute part of that payment to participating practices and keep part. The company's public materials describe sharing rewards with partners but do not publish the split percentage, and practice-level contract terms are not public, so any specific split should be treated as unverified. A third-party profile states that Aledade does not charge membership fees, but this is not confirmed in a company document reviewed here. Because CMS reconciles MSSP savings well after a performance year ends, there is a long lag between when Aledade spends to support practices and when savings are paid. Aledade said in December 2025 that a new $500 million credit facility helps it bridge that Medicare payment timing gap and speed shared-savings distributions to clinicians. Aledade also runs Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and commercial value-based contracts (200+ contracts per its February 2026 fact sheet), some of which may involve downside risk at the ACO level.

facts.primary_revenue: share of shared savings from value-based contracts (MSSP, MA, Medicaid, commercial)

title: Pearl Health: overview and model
questions: What is Pearl Health?
How does Pearl Health work with primary care practices?
Is Pearl Health an ACO?
summary: Pearl Health, founded in 2020, is a technology-led value-based care enablement company for primary care. It operates Pearl-affiliated ACOs that practices join, initially centered on CMS's ACO REACH model and later expanding to the Medicare Shared Savings Program and Medicare Advantage partnerships (first MA partnerships in 2024). Pearl pairs a software platform, which delivers predictive clinical signals and alerts into practice and EHR workflows, with risk-bearing and program administration. Partners include independent practices, physician networks, health systems and other ACOs. Michael Kopko is co-founder and CEO. In its January 2026 release, Pearl said it was positioned to support MSSP, CMS's planned LEAD model, and Medicare Advantage strategies. Like Aledade and Wellvana, Pearl does not own clinics; its model differs mainly in its early focus on REACH and its emphasis on software-driven point-of-care alerts.

title: Pearl Health economics in ACO REACH
questions: How do practices get paid in Pearl's ACO REACH program?
What changed in ACO REACH for 2026 for Pearl practices?
Does Pearl offer capitation?
summary: Pearl's REACH guidance tells participating practices that the model gives them primary care capitation payments described as predictable monthly revenue, plus shared savings from the first dollar with no minimum savings rate, judged on four claims-based and survey quality measures (unplanned admissions for multiple chronic conditions, timely follow-up, all-condition readmission, and CAHPS). For performance year 2026, CMS (announced May 21, 2025) narrowed the first Global-track risk corridor from 25% to 10% of benchmark, raised the quality withhold from 2% to 5%, reduced regional weighting in benchmarks, added a 3% cap on risk score growth from 2019 to 2026, moved fully to the V28 HCC model, and excluded two DME supply codes flagged for suspect billing from 2024 settlement. Pearl's materials do not publish how savings or losses are divided between the Pearl ACO and practices; contract-level terms are private. CMS has indicated REACH ends after 2026, with LEAD as successor.

facts.practice_payment: primary care capitation (monthly) plus shared savings, per Pearl guidance

summary: Wellvana is a value-based care enablement company founded in 2018 and headquartered in Nashville, Tennessee, led by President and CEO Kyle Wailes. It partners with independent primary care practices, hospitals and health systems, and also works with payers. Wellvana operates multiple ACOs in the Medicare Shared Savings Program across several tracks and has held ACO REACH participation and Medicare Advantage contracts. Its service offering combines onboarding, embedded or guided clinical and operational support, risk adjustment and documentation help, between-visit patient outreach, and an analytics platform branded Clarity. Wellvana is privately held; CVS Health became a minority investor in March 2025 when Wellvana bought CVS's MSSP business.

summary: agilon health (NYSE: AGL) partners with existing physician groups in its markets to move them into full-risk Medicare Advantage arrangements without the groups selling their practices. agilon forms a local entity with an anchor group, contracts with MA plans for global capitation covering the members attributed to that group's primary care physicians, and supplies capital, data, care management and payer contracting. title: How agilon health makes money: percent-of-premium capitation
questions: How does agilon make money?
What is percent of premium capitation?
What risk does agilon take?
Does agilon cover Part D?
summary: agilon's revenue is overwhelmingly medical services revenue from Medicare Advantage payers. Under global capitation it receives a per-member-per-month fee that is typically a defined percentage of the premium the MA plan receives from CMS for members attributed to agilon's partner PCPs. In exchange it is financially responsible for essentially all Part A and B costs (hospital, facility, primary and specialty physician and ancillary services) and, in some contracts, Part D drug costs. Physician partners share in the surplus. Some contracts add quality bonuses or penalties tied to Star ratings, and premiums are subject to retroactive CMS risk adjustment changes. Because agilon books the full premium as revenue and the full claims as expense, its revenue is large (about $5.9 billion in 2025) relative to its margin, and small swings in cost trend or risk-adjustment revenue move profitability sharply. agilon reports 'medical margin' (capitation revenue minus medical services expense) as a key metric.

title: agilon health medical margin collapse 2023-2025
questions: Why did agilon health stock fall?
What happened to agilon's medical margin?
Is agilon profitable?
Why are full-risk MA providers losing money?
summary: agilon's results deteriorated as Medicare Advantage cost trends rose and risk-adjustment revenue softened. It cut 2023 guidance in November 2023 after raising reserves for claims incurred but not reported, and in January 2024 lowered its 2023 medical margin outlook by about $110 million (as summarized in a securities-litigation notice). Medical margin fell from about $299 million in 2023 to $205 million in 2024 and to a loss of about $57 million in 2025, per the FY2025 10-K. In Q2 2025 it reported a medical margin loss and withdrew full-year guidance, and its CEO departed; press reports cited prior-period cost development and a risk-adjustment revenue shortfall, and shares fell sharply. Full-year 2025 net loss was $391 million and adjusted EBITDA was negative $296 million, with $285 million of cash and marketable securities against $35 million debt. For 2026 it guided to $300-350 million medical margin and roughly breakeven adjusted EBITDA, citing exits, reduced Part D exposure and about $35 million of 2025 operating cost cuts.

summary: On August 4, 2025, agilon announced that CEO Steven Sell had left and that co-founder and chairman Ronald A. Williams became Executive Chairman, leading an Office of the Chairman on an interim basis while the board searched for a permanent CEO; guidance was suspended. On April 27, 2026, agilon named Tim O'Rourke CEO effective May 7, 2026, a former Humana executive of 17 years who had led Help at Home and Ascension Complete, with Williams continuing as chairman. The reset includes exiting unprofitable markets and payer contracts, reducing Part D exposure to under 15% of membership, slowing new-geography entry (about $15 million of 2026 entry costs), and placing some members in a no-downside care-coordination fee model. On the CMS side, agilon moved three ACOs from REACH to MSSP for 2026 and said participation in CMS's planned LEAD model, which replaces REACH in 2027, depends on unresolved details.

summary: Privia Health Group (Nasdaq: PRVA) is a physician enablement company that combines a management services organization (MSO) with a single-TIN medical group in each market and physician-led ACOs. Physicians join their local Privia Medical Group, typically as owners under the standard model (or through non-owned friendly groups where state law requires), while keeping their practices. The local MSO handles revenue cycle, technology, administrative and operational work, and Privia's payer contracting team negotiates fee-for-service and value-based contracts across commercial, Medicare Advantage, MSSP and Medicaid. Unlike Aledade, Privia sits inside the practice's fee-for-service revenue stream as well as its value-based contracts; unlike agilon, it is primarily multi-payer and only partly at full risk. It describes over 1,300 practices and 5,300+ physicians and advanced practitioners (early 2026).

summary: Privia's GAAP revenue includes fee-for-service revenue billed through its medical groups plus value-based revenue (shared savings, care management fees and capitation-type payments). title: Oak Street Health: owned-clinic senior primary care model

summary: Oak Street Health, founded in 2012 and based in Chicago, operates its own primary care centers for Medicare-eligible adults, often in lower-income neighborhoods, employing its clinicians and care teams. Its economics depend on value-based capitation: Medicare Advantage plans (and, before 2023, CMS's Direct Contracting model, succeeded by ACO REACH) pay Oak Street a monthly amount per at-risk patient, and Oak Street bears responsibility for the patient's total medical costs. Its FY2022 10-K reported that fee-for-service made up less than 1% of revenue, and it tracked 'patient contribution' (capitated revenue minus medical claims expense) as its core unit metric, which improves as patients stay longer. Payer concentration was high: Humana accounted for 32% of 2022 capitated revenue, and the top three payers about 55%. CVS Health acquired Oak Street in May 2023, and it now operates within CVS's Health Care Delivery business as a multi-payer provider.

summary: ChenMed is a privately held, Chen family-owned primary care company based in Miami that runs its own senior medical centers for Medicare-eligible, mostly lower- to moderate-income older adults with chronic conditions. Its brands include Chen Senior Medical Center, Dedicated Senior Medical Center and JenCare Senior Medical Center, plus InTune Health. Founder James Chen began in primary care practice in Miami Gardens; his son Christopher Chen is CEO. ChenMed does not publish financial statements.

summary: VillageMD is a primary care company that operated the Village Medical clinics, many co-located inside Walgreens stores, and later the Summit Health and CityMD multispecialty and urgent care businesses. title: Aledade vs agilon health: two value-based models
questions: What's the difference between Aledade and agilon?

summary: Aledade and agilon both leave physicians independent, but they sit at opposite ends of the risk spectrum. Aledade organizes many small independent practices and health centers into ACOs, earning mostly from shared savings in Traditional Medicare (MSSP) plus MA, Medicaid and commercial contracts; CMS pays only if spending comes in below a benchmark, and losses in two-sided tracks are capped, so revenue is lumpy and delayed but downside is bounded. agilon instead partners with larger anchor physician groups under typically 20-year agreements and takes global capitation from MA plans as a percentage of premium, booking the whole premium as revenue (about $5.9 billion in 2025) and bearing all Part A/B and sometimes Part D costs. That gives agilon far larger revenue per member but full exposure to cost trend and risk-adjustment changes: its medical margin swung from about $299 million (2023) to a loss of about $57 million (2025), while Aledade reported over $1 billion of 2024 MSSP savings (company-reported).

title: Owned-clinic senior primary care vs practice enablement
questions: What's the difference between Oak Street and Aledade?
Owned clinics vs enablement in value-based care
Why are senior primary care clinic chains struggling?
summary: Two main business models dominate value-based primary care. Owned-clinic operators (Oak Street Health, ChenMed, VillageMD) build or buy centers, employ clinicians and usually take full Medicare Advantage risk. They control care delivery tightly but need heavy capital, years for new centers to fill panels, and depend on a few MA payers; Humana was 32% of Oak Street's 2022 capitated revenue. Since 2023 this model has shown strain: CVS took a ~$5.7 billion impairment and closed 16 Oak Street centers, Walgreens booked a $12.4 billion gross VillageMD impairment and closed about 160 clinics, and ChenMed churned CEOs. Enablement companies (Aledade, Pearl Health, Wellvana, Privia) leave practices independent and supply technology, staff, contracting and an ACO or medical-group wrapper. They are capital-light and scale faster across thousands of practices, but control care less directly and often earn delayed, variable shared-savings income.

title: Enablement economics: who bears downside risk
questions: Who bears the downside risk in an ACO enablement deal?
Do practices lose money in value-based care with an enabler?
How do enablers like Aledade, Pearl and Privia fund operations?
summary: Downside risk sits in different places depending on model. In MSSP and REACH, the legal ACO entity contracts with CMS and owes any shared losses; when an enabler sponsors the ACO (Aledade, Pearl, Wellvana, Privia's ACOs), the enabler typically funds or backstops that risk, while practice-level terms, including whether practices share losses, are private and not disclosed in public materials. In MA percent-of-premium deals (agilon), the company carries full medical cost risk on its balance sheet and shares surplus with physician groups; agilon's losses in 2024-2025 show where that risk landed. Owned-clinic operators (Oak Street, ChenMed) bear it directly. Because CMS pays savings months after a performance year, enablers lean on credit: Aledade's $500 million Ares facility (2025) and Pearl's $60 million credit line (2026). CMS policy can also shift risk, e.g., REACH's 2026 narrower risk corridor and higher quality withhold.
